full_judgment:
6. In the course or submissions a point was raised as to the language used in section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the scope of an application under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the issuance of writ of Habeas Corpus within the meaning of section 491 of the Code. We find that the phrases whenever it thinks fit forms a part of section 491 and those expressions go to mean that a High Court has discretion in the matter as regards the nature of the order to be passed and it also emphasises that the High Court may pass an order under this section at any time. The phrases illegally or improperly used in the section (b) of section 491 of the Code mean that-when a person is not detained within the provisions of any law the detention becomes an illegal detention. The expression improperly, however, has a wider connotation than the word illegally and in our opinion the word improperly refers to cases in which although the forms of law have been observed but there has been a fraud on an act or an abuse of the process of the powers given to the executive by the legislature and in such cases it is the duly of the Court to step in and order the detenu to be set at liberty and an order of detention passed on fictitious and colorable satisfaction and without care or circumspection commensurate with gravity of the case affecting the liberty of the citizen must never be sustained by any court. A similar view was taken although from a different perspective in the case of Kripasindu Hazra Vs. The state in criminal Miscellaneous case No. 69 of 1977 where a Division Bench of this Court in summing up of the scope of section 491 of the Code has held that the scope of section 491 is wider than the constitutional provision. 

 7. The next question that has been raised by Mr. Serajul Huq, the learned Advocate is the scope of Rule 30 and Rule 5(1) of the Emergency Powers Rules. It is apparent from the plain reading of Rule 30 as has been submitted by Mr. Serajul Huq the learned Advocate, that the powers exercised under Rule 30 are special power and detention of a person by this power is a temporary power of detention as is evident from the provision of sub-Rule (2). In sub-rule (2) it is clear that a person at the maximum could be detained for a period of two months. Rule 5(1)(a) is to be read with clause (VIII) of section 2(2) of the Emergency Powers Act under which these rules arc framed. Rule 5(1)(a) permits the detention of a person on the grounds stated in rule 5(1) for an indefinite period of time. The question, however, comes for our decision is that under what circumstances an order under Rule 5(1)(a) is warranted. We find that the temporary detention is permissible under rule 30 and the detaining authority must consider the circumstances of the case to be reasonable and necessary enough to pass an order of temporary detention. This is evident from the clear language used in sub-rule (3) of Rule 30 which runs as follows: 

 " On receipt of any report made, under the provision of sub-rule (2), the Government may, in addition to making such order, subject to the proviso to sub-rule (2) , as may appear to be necessary for the temporary custody of any person arrested under this rule, make in exercise of any power conferred upon it by any law for the time being in force such final order as to his detention release, residence or any other matter concerning him as may appear to it in the circumstance of the case to be reasonable or necessary." 

 From this Mr. Serajul Huq has submitted that in passing the order of detention under rule 5(1) the detaining authority’s satisfaction must be based upon the reasonableness of the materials and the necessity for making such order of detention. For this proposition Mr. Serajul Huq has relied upon the decision in the case of the Government of West Pakistan versus Begum Agha Abdul Karim Shorish Kashmiri reported in 21 D.L.R. S.C. Page I. Mr. Serajul Huq the learned Advocate has submitted that their Lordships of the Supreme Court were considering the question of satisfaction in the exercise of their constitutional jurisdiction. He has also submitted that the standard of satisfaction which is required in the exercise of jurisdiction under the constitutional guarantees arc the same as in the case of an application filed under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Mr. K.A. Wahab, the learned Deputy Advocate-General has frankly submitted that the materials upon which such satisfaction is to be derived by the detaining authority must be such that it shall satisfy a reasonable mind. 

 8. A further question comes for no consideration in this case is that the detaining authority under rule 5(1) is to be satisfied with respect to any person with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the security, the public safety or interest of Bangladesh, Bangladesh's relation with any foreign power, the maintenance of public order, the maintenance of peaceful conditions in any part of Bangladesh, or the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the life of the community it is necessary so to do, and then may make an order (a) directing that such person be detained. 

 9. Before this direction for detention is passed by the detaining authority the detaining authority must exercise its independent reasonable mind as has been given in scheme of these rule". Reading rule 30 giving the powers to the police to arrest a person whom the Police Officer concerned reasonably suspects of having acted or being about to act in a manner prejudicial to the security, the public safety or interest of Bangladesh or the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the life of the community, to make a report to the Government within a period not exceeding fifteen days and thereupon, the Government may pass an order if satisfied upon the materials submitted before it to detain the person concerned in sub-rule 2 for a period of two months or under rule 5(I)(a) for an indefinite period of time. Reading of section 30 and Rule 5 clearly indicate that the functions of the Government for the purpose of passing an order of detention have been divided into two stages. The first stage is the function of the police officer who is to arrest upon a reasonable suspicion of having acted in a manner prejudicial etc. The materials, thereafter, go to the Government who is to apply its independent mind as it is evident both from the language used under sub-rule 3 of Rule 30, as will as Rule 5. Sub-rule 3 speaks of an order being passed if it appears in the circumstances of the case to be reasonable or necessary. In rule 5 if the Government is satisfied with respect to such person, then an order is to be passed for detention. The fancies as given to the police officer under rule (1) of Rule 30 and function of the Government as contemplated in Rule 5 and sub-rule 3 of Rule 30 must not be- confused as overlapping each other as they are quite independent of one another. At the first stage police on reasonable suspicion makes the arrest and if the person it to be detained beyond the period of 15 days the materials are submitted to the Government for its independent application of mind. In the exercise of its power the Government has delegated the authority of passing the order of detention to various functionaries of the Government. In the instant case-the delegated authority are the District Magistrate or the Additional District Magistrates. The Government having delegated its authority to the District Magistrate and the Additional District Magistrate also clearly indicate that in order to derive satisfaction the Magistrate is not merely to act as an Executive authority but is also to act as a Magistrate which means that the delegated authority namely the Division Magistrate or the Additional District Magistrate must apply the legal standard for the purpose of deriding the subjective satisfaction. It is very significant that the power of detention has been given to the maximum of 15 days to the police officer. The legislature has not given the power for indefinite detention' upon a police officer and this is commensurate with the Code of Criminal Procedure. If a person is detained under the provision of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the obligation of the appropriate authority is to produce the accused before a Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest for committing, suspecting to have committed a crime in one of the provision of Penal Code or any other criminal legislation. When the Police arrests a person for having acted or is about to act in a manner prejudicial to the Slate the order of detention is used to the maximum for a parboil of 15 days. After the action, the person is either to be detained temporarily beyond the period of 15 days or maximum period of 2 months or indefinitely. It is the Government who has to pass that order and not the police Officer. The Government, for the purpose of passing such order, as we have already noted has delegated its authority to the Additional District Magistrate or District Magistrate. In our opinion this delegation of the authority for detaining a person is clearly enough to point out, that as under the Criminal Procedure Code, the Magistrate while disposing of an accused produced before him exercises his judicial mind within the frame work of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which means that the police must within a reasonable time produce before it sufficient materials which will satisfy the legal mind of the Magistrate to keep the accused concerned in custody till submission of the police report under sec. 173 of the Code by the police after investigation. The same standard is also to be applied by the Additional District Magistrate because of the fact that the delegated authority is to be satisfied and this satisfaction is the satisfaction of a legally trained mind and not of an automation entrusting the report submitted by the Executive i.e. the police. 

 10. From this if we consider the present case before us we find that the police officer after having arrested the detenu on 12.2.76 under Rule 30 of the Emergency Powers Rules presumably on collection of materials forwarded the materials to the Additional District Magistrate who by his order dated 25.2.76 passed the order of detention under Rule 5(1)(a) of the Emergency Powers Rule for detention of the detenu for an indefinite period of time. 

 11. In the counter-affidavit filed on behalf of the State it has been stated as we have quoted, in para 5 that after the 15th of August, 1975 the detenu organised (1) Espionage (2) maintained liaison with India and (3) collected men for sending them to India for training them for overthrowing the present regime. The materials placed before us by the learned Deputy Advocate-General are three letters from different sources. These letters, we must say, are not only vague but also lack mateials to connect the three times mentioned above which would warrant satisfaction as is to be derived under Rule 5(I). The materials which are needed for the purpose of being satisfied are the materials which are contemplated under section 106 of the Evidence Act. In the unreported decision of Kripasindu Hazra which we have already referred to has also spoken of the materials to prove bonafide as contemplated in section 106 of the Evident Act and the same has also been .spoken in the case reported in 21 D.L.R. S.c. page 1. We have nothing in these letters beyond making vague references to certain unidentified persons and meetings of which also no date nor any other particulars arc to be found. These letters have been relied upon as the materials for the satisfaction of the Additional District Magistrate. We have in vain looked for the materials in the file of the Additional District Magistrate to see how he applied his independent mind as a Magistrate in the case but we are told that there is no such file or order excepting the order by which the detenu has been detained. It has been submitted by the learned Deputy Advocate General that beyond this order there is nothing on record to show that the Additional District Magistrate had passed any other order. The learned Deputy-Advocate-General has pointed out to a note in the file which is to the effect that the detenu may be detained under the provision of section 5(1)(a) of the Emergency Powers Rules. This note has been given by the Deputy Superintendent of police of the Special Branch Dhaka City. This is dated 24.2.76. Under this signature the Additional District Magistrate has put his initial with the date 25.2.76. In a separate sheet an independent order has been passed which is the order served on the detenu. We have already pointed out that this sort of countersigning the report. of the police officer is not contemplated by the legislature in passing an order under section 5(1)(a) of the Rule and the order passed on such satisfaction in our opinion is a colourable satisfaction and is not contemplated within the frame work of Rule 5(1). We have already pointed out that the legislature clearly intended the delegated authority to apply his independent legal mind before passing an order of detention and not to act as a automation. In the circumstances we find that the order of detention has not been passed in accordance with Rule 5(I)(a) and it must be set aside. 

 12. In the result the Rule is made absolute and we direct that the detenu be set at liberty forthwith if not wanted in connection with any other case.
